transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-12 14:30 PT
Duration: ~52m
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Omar Patel (Redwood SE), Janelle Ortiz (Acme CTO), Ravi Desai (Acme ML Eng), Marta Li (Acme PM)
---
[00:00:04] Maya: hey everyone thanks for joining, um we'll keep this tight, goal is to scope the POC success criteria around latency and throughput - TTFT vs T P O T, p95/p99 targets and how we'll measure them.
[00:00:18] Janelle: sounds good, thanks Maya. we mainly want this for our customer-facing chat assistant, 95% of interactions are short question answer, but we do have long form summarization in some flows.
[00:00:33] Omar: perfect. quick context check - is the initial POC on Hosted API or Dedicated?
[00:00:38] Ravi: we'd like to validate Dedicated first, because we need predictable throughput and data isolation. but if latency is markedly better on hosted, we'd consider hybrid.
[00:00:48] Marta: timeline wise leadership wants a decision within 4 weeks, so a 2-3 week technical POC works.
[00:00:55] Maya: great. so first off definitions — Omar, can you run TTFT vs TPOT?
[00:01:00] Omar: sure. so, TTFT — time to first token — measures how long from request arrival until the first token is emitted. it's critical for perceived latency in chat. TPOT, as we discussed, we'll use to mean time-per-output-token (time to generate each subsequent token); some folks call it TPT but in this doc we'll use TPOT to match Acme's notes. TPOT captures how fast we can stream responses and affects throughput.
[00:01:28] Janelle: ok that matches our mental model. we care most about p95 TTFT for UX, and p99 for SLOs. for cost planning we want tokens/sec and also p95 TPOT numbers.
[00:01:39] Omar: good. suggested baseline targets for chat: p95 TTFT <= 200ms and p99 <= 400ms for 32-128 token prompts with short outputs (~32 tokens). for TPOT, p95 <= 25ms/token and p99 <= 45ms/token on Dedicated with an optimized config. those are initial targets we can tune.
[00:01:57] Ravi: those p95 numbers sound ambitious but plausible. how will we account for cold starts, kv cache misses, and batching effects?
[00:02:08] Omar: we'll separate measurement buckets: cold-start TTFT (first request after model load), warm TTFT (with KV cache warmed and no batching), batched TPOT at different batch sizes, and end-to-end TPOT under simulated concurrency. also measure prefix caching where applicable.
[00:02:24] Marta: how do you simulate real traffic? our production has a lot of short bursts, spiky concurrency up to ~70 concurrent sessions with a median request size 60 tokens and output 40 tokens.
[00:02:35] Maya: perfect, that's the kind of distribution we need. in the measurement plan we'll use your target distribution: prompt length buckets [32 (30%), 128 (50%), 512 (20%)] and output lengths [32 (60%), 256 (40%)], concurrency profiles [1, 8, 16, 32, 64].
[00:02:50] [00:03:02] Janelle: and we need to understand both TTFT and tokens/sec at 95th percentile because that drives perceived lag and cost respectively.
[00:03:10] Omar: right. proposed metrics: TTFT p50/p95/p99, TPOT p50/p95/p99, tokens-per-second (aggregate), requests-per-second, GPU util, memory pressure, and error rates. we'll also collect sequence length conditioned latency.
[00:03:26] Ravi: what's the recommended sample size? we want statistically meaningful p99s.
[00:03:31] Omar: for p99 you generally need thousands of samples per config. our perf harness will run ~5k requests per config or 10 minutes of steady-state traffic per point, whichever comes first, and then we aggregate.
[00:03:43] Marta: will the harness account for network latency vs pure inference time?
[00:03:47] Omar: yes we'll measure both edge-to-edge (client request to first token seen by client) and server-side model-inference time. we'll provide both raw server latencies and synthetic client-latencies with a representative network emulation.
[00:03:58] Maya: let's talk SLO thresholds for the POC pass/fail. suggested acceptance criteria:
[00:04:03] Maya (cont): - For conversation flows: TTFT p95 <= 250ms, TTFT p99 <= 450ms; TPOT p95 <= 30ms/token; overall error rate < 0.1% and GPU util under 90% at target concurrency.
[00:04:19] Janelle: why are these slightly looser than Omar suggested earlier?
[00:04:22] Omar: we added margin to reflect representative production variability and network emulation; the narrower numbers we quoted earlier are optimistic tuned configs. POC acceptance should allow some buffer.
[00:04:30] Ravi: for summarization (long outputs), what's reasonable?
[00:04:33] Omar: for long form outputs (256 tokens), expect TPOT to dominate. suggested target: p95 TPOT <= 40ms/token and end-to-end tokens/sec at p95 >= 2000 tokens/sec aggregated across the Dedicated pool.
[00:04:45] Marta: we'll need cost estimates mapped to these throughput numbers.
[00:04:48] Maya: we'll include cost per 1M tokens and an estimate for your expected QPS given your distribution.
[00:04:53] [00:05:10] Janelle: measurement plan specifics please — steps and instrumentation.
[00:05:14] Omar: plan outline: 1) Acme provides prompt set + length distribution and target concurrency matrix. 2) Redwood seeds Dedicated dev pool with the model variant (quantized vs fp16) — we will test both. 3) Run warm-up phase to populate KV cache (5-10 minutes). 4) Run steady-state tests across concurrency points with our harness collecting TTFT/TPOT/RPS/TPS. 5) Run cold-start tests where we restart a node and measure first request latency. 6) Run scale tests (vertical/horizontal) to understand throughput vs GPU count. 7) Produce a report with per-config p50/p95/p99 plus system metrics and cost extrapolation.
[00:06:00] Ravi: how will we handle batching? our app is real-time so small batch sizes, but I'm curious about optional batching for background tasks.
[00:06:07] Omar: we'll run configs with batch sizes [1, 4, 8, 16] and also test continuous batching (where runtime accumulates small amounts for a few ms). we'll report the latency distribution for each.
[00:06:20] Marta: can we capture trace-level info to map latency to model internals?
[00:06:23] Omar: yes — we'll enable tracing hooks and token-level timestamps so you can correlate stall points and kernel times. note tracing may add small overhead.
[00:06:31] Maya: ok on tooling — we'll share the harness repo link, a spreadsheet with configs, and an initial Jenkins GH action example. Omar, confirm you'll include instructions for on-prem or VPC runs?
[00:06:40] Omar: yes I'll include both; for VPC we provide a config to run the harness from your VPC to avoid crossing public internet.
[00:06:46] Janelle: about model variants and quantization — we need accuracy checks as well. performance without quality is meaningless for us.
[00:06:51] Omar: totally. we'll run accuracy/regression checks using your labeled dev set alongside perf runs. we'll include automated evals (ROUGE/EM or custom metrics) and flag any quality regressions.
[00:07:02] Ravi: are there common gotchas with KV cache or streaming that inflate TTFT?
[00:07:07] Omar: yes. cold KV cache and model loading cause big TTFT spikes; also some orchestration during autoscaling can add jitter. we recommend dedicated warm pools for latency-sensitive flows and a fallback to a slightly lower-cost tier for bulk workloads.
[00:07:21] Marta: what's the POC timeline again?
[00:07:24] Maya: proposed 3-week split: week1: config + harness and prompt handoff; week2: run benchmarks (warm/cold, concurrency, batch variations) and mid-week results call; week3: follow-up runs for tuned configs, cost extrapolation, and final report + decision criteria.
[00:07:39] Janelle: that fits leadership needs.
[00:07:42] [00:08:00] Omar: one more note on measurement fidelity — to reliably measure p99 we need to control noise: run tests in isolation on the Dedicated dev pool (no other tenants), ensure stable network, and do multiple runs to get confidence intervals. we'll show median and 95% CI for p95/p99.
[00:08:18] Ravi: do you simulate token streaming client-side?
[00:08:21] Omar: yes the harness will simulate streaming clients and timestamp each token event for TPOT measurement.
[00:08:27] Marta: what's the acceptance gate for cost?
[00:08:30] Maya: we'll provide cost per 1M tokens for each config and map to your projected monthly token volume; the business gate will be a combination of meeting latency SLOs and being within target TCO (we'll produce a few scenarios).
[00:08:42] Janelle: any security/compliance blockers for running the harness in our VPC?
[00:08:46] Omar: we support running the harness inside your VPC; we'll hand over a read-only role and minimal network egress. for Private on-prem deployments we can provide a containerized harness.
[00:08:56] [00:09:10] Maya: ok let's capture the concrete POC pass criteria so we all agree:
[00:09:14] Maya (cont): 1) Conversation flow TTFT p95 <= 250ms and p99 <= 450ms; 2) TPOT p95 <= 30ms/token for short outputs and p95 <= 40ms/token for long outputs; 3) End-to-end throughput at target concurrency with GPU util < 90%; 4) No regression on accuracy beyond agreed margin (e.g., delta < 2% on key evals); 5) Cost per 1M tokens within agreed budget scenario.
[00:09:47] Janelle: agreed, will take that back to procurement and ops.
[00:09:51] [00:10:12] Omar: logistical notes — we'll need ssh access for on-prem, a service account for VPC harness, and your sample prompts. we'll draft a checklist.
[00:10:21] Ravi: can Redwood run an initial smoke benchmark on your infra so we have a sanity check before our run?
[00:10:25] Omar: yes we'll run a smoke on the Dedicated dev pool and share the logs and raw traces.
[00:10:30] Marta: final Q — how do we interpret p99 outliers caused by autoscaler? do we penalize that?
[00:10:35] Omar: we'll annotate runs — if autoscaler-induced restarts caused p99 spikes, we'll separate those and show both 'steady-state' and 'observed' metrics. POC acceptance focuses on steady-state for the SLO but we also document observed behavior and mitigation.
[00:10:49] Maya: awesome. quick recap of next steps: Maya will send pricing/terms and the POC checklist; Omar will send harness + runbook; Ravi will share prompts and distribution; we'll schedule benchmark week of 3/24.
[00:11:01] Janelle: thanks everyone.
[00:11:03] Maya: thanks — we'll follow up in email and drive to the action items.
[00:11:07] [End of recorded transcript — remainder of meeting was scheduling details and calendar invites]
